# Theory on hydropower - from setup to efficiency

## Layout of a hydropower plant

A hydropower plant converts the potential and kinetic energy of water into electricity. Below is a practical, skimmable layout from upstream to grid:

- Reservoir or river reach: Stores or channels water; sets available head and flow.
- Dam and intake structure: Gates, trash racks, and screens keep debris out.
- Headrace tunnel/canal: Conveys water from intake; often includes a surge tank to absorb pressure transients.
- Penstock: High-pressure pipe carrying water to the turbine; designed for head, flow, and water hammer.
- Turbine: Converts water energy to shaft power. Common types:
  - Pelton: high head, low flow (impulse).
  - Francis: medium head/flow (reaction).
  - Kaplan/Propeller: low head, high flow (reaction, adjustable blades).
- Draft tube: Recovers kinetic energy and discharges water to tailrace.
- Generator: Converts mechanical shaft power to electrical power.
- Transformer and switchgear: Steps up voltage; protection and interconnection.
- Tailrace: Returns water to the river; avoid submergence/backpressure.
- Spillway and bypasses: Safely pass floods without using the turbine.
- Control & auxiliaries: Governors, AVR/excitation, protection, lubrication, cooling, HVAC, monitoring.

End-to-end flow sequence:
1) Upstream water level provides head.
2) Intake opens; water passes screens.
3) Headrace/penstock conveys flow; surge tank limits pressure spikes.
4) Turbine converts water energy; governor sets speed/power.
5) Generator produces electricity; AVR holds voltage/reactive power.
6) Transformer steps up to grid voltage; breakers connect to substation.
7) Tailrace returns water downstream.

Key performance relation:

$$P = \rho\, g\, Q\, H\, \eta$$

Where: $\rho$ is water density (~1000 kg/m³), $g$ is 9.81 m/s², $Q$ is flow (m³/s), $H$ is net head (m), and $\eta$ is overall efficiency (turbine × generator × mechanical).

Example: If H = 50 m, Q = 20 m³/s, and $\eta = 0.9$, then $P \approx 1000 \times 9.81 \times 20 \times 50 \times 0.9 \approx 8.8$ MW.

Variants to know:
- Storage (reservoir) plants: Energy buffering, peaking, flood control, irrigation.
- Run-of-river: Minimal storage; high efficiency, lower flexibility.
- Pumped-storage: Two reservoirs; pump up off-peak, generate on-peak (grid-scale storage).

## How a power plant works (general)

Common building blocks across technologies:
- Primary energy: Water head/flow, fuel chemical energy, wind kinetic energy, solar irradiance, geothermal heat, nuclear fission.
- Prime mover: Turbine (hydraulic/steam/gas), engine, or none for PV.
- Generator and excitation: Converts shaft power to electricity; AVR controls voltage/reactive power.
- Grid interface: Transformers, breakers, relays; power electronics as needed (inverters/converters).
- Controls: Governor (frequency/active power), AVR (voltage/reactive), start/stop, ramping, safety interlocks.
- Balance-of-plant: Cooling, lubrication, fuel/water handling, filtration, HVAC, fire protection, drainage, monitoring.

Operational objectives:
- Support frequency (active power) and voltage (reactive power).
- Dispatch per operator/market with ramp and limit compliance.
- Protect assets (faults, overloads, transients).
- Coordinate syncing, islanding, and black start (where applicable).

## Technology snapshots and differences

- Hydropower: High efficiency, fast response, low OPEX; site-dependent, environmental constraints; strong for peaking/regulation.
- Thermal (coal/gas/biomass): Fuel → boiler/combustor → steam/gas turbine → generator; slower ramp (steam), emissions/fuel logistics.
- Nuclear: Steam cycle from reactor heat; high availability, low marginal cost; baseload with stringent safety systems.
- Wind: Rotor → gearbox/direct-drive → generator → converter; variable output; forecasting and grid-forming inverters help.
- Solar PV: Modules → DC → inverter → AC; no rotating mass; power electronics handle grid support; zero fuel cost, variable output.
- Geothermal: Flash/binary cycles using hot brines; steady baseload where resources permit.

## Efficiency and losses (hydro focus)

- Hydraulic: Intake, bends, friction, penstock, draft tube.
- Turbine: Peak near design point; manage off-design losses and cavitation via runner/wicket-gate optimization.
- Mechanical/electrical: Bearings, seals, generator copper/iron, transformer losses.
- Debris/sediment: Screens and desanders reduce wear and performance degradation.

Rule-of-thumb turbine mapping:
- Pelton: head > 300 m, lower flows.
- Francis: head ~ 30–300 m, medium flows.
- Kaplan/Propeller/Bulb: head < 30 m, high flows.

## Quick glossary

- Head (H): Vertical difference between upstream water level and turbine discharge (net head after losses).
- Flow (Q): Water volume rate through turbine.
- Capacity factor: Actual energy vs. if at rated power 100% of the time.
- Governor: Controls turbine gates/nozzles for power/speed.
- AVR: Automatic Voltage Regulator for generator excitation.
